pages.lead: Here is how to quote a job in the right order, from the first phone call to a quote the customer can accept. One garden fence job runs through every step.
pages.answer: To quote a job, first find out exactly what the customer wants. Price the materials, your time, your overheads and your profit. Write one clear quote and send it the same day or the next morning. The quote needs a short scope, a total, what is not included, payment terms and a valid-until date. pages.content:
Get the details before you price anything

Do the asking before the pricing. A price built on a guess ends up too low for you or too high for the customer.

On the first call, ask these questions and write down the answers.

  • What do you want done, in your own words?
  • Where is the job, and how easy is it to reach with tools and materials?
  • What is there now, and does all of it come out?
  • Does the work need a permit, or anyone's permission, such as a landlord or a neighbour?
  • Is anything still undecided, like colours, styles or finishes?
  • Is there a date you must hit, or a budget in mind?
  • Who decides, and who pays?
  • When can I come and look?

At the visit, measure everything and take photos of what is there. Look for anything that could cost extra, such as poor access, hard ground or old work that hides a problem. If you cannot visit, ask for photos and measurements, and give an estimate until you have seen the job.

Then write the job in your own words and send it to the customer to confirm. Two or three lines are enough: what you will do and what you will not do. A misunderstanding caught now costs one message. Caught halfway through the job, it costs days.

Decide between a fixed quote and an estimate

In plain terms, a quote is a firm price and an estimate is your best guess. Rules for each differ from place to place, so check the ones where you work.

  • Give a fixed quote when you can see and measure the whole job. The customer gets one price, and you carry the risk if the work takes longer.
  • Give an estimate when you cannot know the size of the job until you start, as with fault-finding or repairs behind a wall. Say what could move the price.
  • Use a provisional sum when only one part of the job is unknown. Give it its own line, say what it covers, and settle it at the real cost once you know.
  • Offer options when the customer has not chosen between two ways of doing something. Price each option on its own line.

Whichever you choose, say so on the document. Put the word Quotation or Estimate at the top, and list anything that could change the price. A customer who was told the price could move is easier to deal with when it does.

Price the job in four parts

Every job price has four parts. Work out each one, then add them up.

  • Materials: everything you need, at today's supplier prices, plus waste and delivery.
  • Labour: the hours the job takes at your hourly rate, including travel, setting up and clearing up.
  • Overheads: the cost of running your business that no customer pays for directly, such as your van, tools and insurance.
  • Profit: what is left for you once every cost is paid.

The sums are in our guide to pricing a job quote, which has a calculator. Work out your price there, then come back to write the quote.

The customer does not need to see your overheads or your profit. They can sit inside your rates, so the quote shows clear lines and still covers your costs.

A worked example from first call to finished quote

The job: replace 12 m (40 ft) of rotten garden fence with new panels on new posts. Here is how to make a quote for it, step by step.

  1. First call. The customer says the old fence is falling down and wants the same height. You ask the questions above. You learn that the fence is theirs, that the side gate stays, and that they want the work done before December.
  2. Site visit. You measure 12 m along the boundary and work out that the new fence needs 7 panels, each 1.83 m (6 ft) wide, and 8 posts. Six panels fall short, so the seventh is cut to fit. The ground is firm, but two old posts look as if they are set in concrete. You take photos of everything.
  3. Scope. You write two lines: take down and remove 12 m of old fence, then set 8 new posts and hang 7 panels, 1.8 m (6 ft) high. The customer replies to confirm.
  4. Fixed price or estimate. Everything is clear except those old post bases. You give a fixed quote, with a provisional sum on its own line for extra digging.
  5. Price. You work out materials, labour, overheads and profit, then turn the result into a few clear lines.
  6. Write and send. You number the quote, date it, add a valid-until date, a deposit and how to accept, then email the PDF the next morning.

This is the finished quote. The prices are examples to replace with your own.

Each line tells the customer something.

  • Panels and posts: the customer can see what they are buying and count it when it arrives.
  • Fixings and delivery: small costs are listed, so none of them turns up later as a surprise.
  • Taking down the old fence: the customer knows you will take it away.
  • Labour: two people for two days shows how long you expect to be there.
  • Provisional sum: an allowance for the one thing you cannot see. It is in the total, and the notes say it is settled at the real cost.
  • VAT and total: tax sits on its own line, so the customer sees the price before and after it.

The quote maker is free and needs no signup. You choose the currency and type your own tax rate, so a US job can use dollars and your local sales tax. The notes are plain text, so the tool does not recalculate them. If you change a line, the currency or the tax, work out the deposit and the balance again and change them in the notes, along with the tax wording.

Write the quote so it can be accepted

A quote the customer can say yes to leaves nothing for them to ask. Put all of this on the page.

  • A quote number, the date and a valid-until date.
  • Your details, the customer's details and the address of the job.
  • One line on the scope, then itemised lines with a quantity, a rate and an amount.
  • Tax on its own line if you charge it, then the total.
  • What is not included, naming anything the customer might assume is in the price.
  • Payment terms: the deposit, when the balance is due and how to pay.
  • How changes are handled: extra work is priced and agreed before you do it.
  • How to accept, in one clear step.

Wording you can copy for each part is in our guide on how to write a professional quote. For the acceptance step, see our quote acceptance wording.

Choose the valid-until date with care. It should give the customer time to decide, and it should end before a rise in your material prices can hurt you. Ask for a deposit when you must buy materials or book dates, and write the amount on the quote.

Send it and follow up

Send the quote the same day, or the next morning at the latest, while the job is fresh in the customer's mind. Download it as a PDF and attach it to your own email, because QuotationMaker does not send emails.

Keep the email short. Give the total, and say whether it includes VAT or tax. Add the valid-until date and how to accept. Email wording you can copy is in our guide on sending a quote to a client.

If you hear nothing, send a short, polite message a few days later, and another before the valid-until date. After that, let the quote lapse.

If the job changes before the customer accepts, send a revised quotation with a new date that says what changed. When the customer says yes, send a quotation confirmation with the start date, so you both have the same plan.

A logo helps the customer recognise your business. The free PDF has a small 'Made with GetQuotationMaker.com' line at the bottom of each page. Pro costs $9, paid once, and removes that line and adds your logo.

Checklist before you press send

Read the quote once as the customer would, then check each of these.

  • The customer's name and the job address are right.
  • The customer has confirmed the scope in writing.
  • The scope says what you will do, in plain words.
  • Every line has a quantity, a rate and an amount, and the amounts add up.
  • Tax is shown on its own line, or the quote says none is charged.
  • Anything the customer might assume is included, but is not, is listed as not included.
  • Any unknown part has its own labelled line or a note.
  • The deposit, the balance and how to pay are written out.
  • The deposit and the balance in the notes match the total.
  • The quote has a number, today's date and a valid-until date.
  • It says how to accept.
  • Your phone number and email are on it, so the customer can ask a question.
  • You have noted a date to follow up if you hear nothing.

faq.q: What is the difference between a quote and an estimate?
faq.a: A quote is a firm price for a defined job. An estimate is your best guess and can change. Say which one you are giving at the top of the document, and check the rules where you work, because they differ from place to place.

faq.q: How long should a quote be valid for?
faq.a: Long enough for the customer to decide, and short enough that a rise in material prices cannot hurt you. The example on this page uses 30 days. Use less time if your supplier's prices change often.

faq.q: Do I show my profit and overheads on the quote?
faq.a: You do not have to. They can sit inside your rates and totals. Show lines the customer can check: materials with quantities, labour as days or hours, and any allowance on its own line.

faq.q: How do I quote a job I cannot see?
faq.a: Ask the customer for photos and measurements, and give an estimate instead of a fixed quote. Say what you based it on, and offer to confirm the price after a visit.

faq.q: What if the work changes after the customer says yes?
faq.a: Tell the customer before you do any extra work, and agree the new price in writing before you start it.

faq.q: Do I need to sign up to make the quote?
faq.a: No. The quote maker is free and has no account. Your business name, email and address are remembered on your own device, so the next quote is faster. It does not send emails, so attach the PDF to your own message.

pages.content:
What to put in the terms of a quote

Terms on a quote should be short. The client reads them before saying yes, so they only need to cover what the client must know to decide. Five clauses answer the questions a client has at that point: valid until, deposit and payment, exclusions, changes and cancellation.

Each section below has wording you can copy, with a note on when to use it. Think of the blocks as a quote terms and conditions template: copy what fits and delete the rest. Square brackets mark the parts you change. Put the finished clauses in the notes box under the line items of your quote. The price and the line items come first, and our guides on how to quote a job and how to write a professional quote cover them.

These notes state your offer clearly. They do not replace a contract. A cap on liability, indemnity, ownership of designs, governing law and late-payment interest all belong in a written contract, and a lawyer is the right person to draft one. Use the blocks here for the notes of a one-page quote, and ask for a contract when the job is large or risky.

Valid until: how long the price stays open

The quote validity period is how long your price stays on offer. After the expiry date the price can change. Give the expiry as a date, such as 20 November 2026. Zigaflow gives the reason: a number of days leaves it open when the count starts, at issue, on receipt or on the day the email was opened. A client and a trader who read it differently tend to find out after prices have moved.

For how long, ShiftFlow suggests starting with 14 to 30 days. For prices or schedules that move fast, it puts the figure at 7 to 14 days. It describes the range as a business decision, and no law or industry standard fixes it. Zigaflow adds that when you sell to another business, no law sets a default period, so your quote decides it.

Valid until

Use on most quotes. Change the date, and keep it as a calendar date.

This quote is valid until [date]. After that date the price may change. If you accept later, we will recheck the price and confirm it in writing first.

Valid until, when material prices move

Use when the price depends on supplier costs that change often. Pick a shorter date.

Material prices change often. This quote is valid until [date]. After that date we will recheck the cost of materials before we confirm the price.

An expiry date on its own does not hold a start date for the client. ShiftFlow says the date only shows when you will look at your price and availability again. If you want to hold dates for the client, tie them to a step such as the deposit, and say so in the deposit wording below.

If the date passes and the client then says yes, treat the old quote as closed. Recheck your costs and your availability, then send a revised quotation with a new date.

Sources checked 30 October 2026: ShiftFlow: How long should a contractor quote be valid?; Zigaflow: Quotation validity.

Deposit and payment terms

Say how much you ask for up front, when the rest is due and how to pay. Write the deposit as an amount, so the client sees the sum they will transfer. Work it out from your own costs: it should cover the materials you must buy and the dates you hold.

Deposit and balance

Use on short jobs where you buy materials or book dates. Change both amounts so they add up to the total.

Deposit: [deposit amount] is due when you accept this quote. It books [start date] and pays for the materials we order.

The balance of [balance amount] is due [when, for example on completion].

On a longer job, split the price into stages. Tie each stage to something the client can see, such as the delivery of materials or the end of the first week.

Payment in stages

Use on jobs that run for weeks. Name each stage by something the client can check.

Payment is in [number] stages.

[Amount] is due when you accept this quote. [Amount] is due when [stage, for example the materials are delivered]. The balance of [amount] is due when the job is finished.

Payment due date and method

Put this after the deposit wording. Keep your bank details on the invoice.

Invoices are due [number] days after the invoice date. Pay by [method, for example bank transfer] and use the invoice number as the reference.

Once the client says yes, send a quotation confirmation that repeats the total, the deposit and the start date.

Exclusions and assumptions

A client sees one total and reads it as the whole job. Tell them what is not in it. Name the things they might expect to find in the price, and add one sentence that closes the gap: anything not listed is not included.

Exclusions

List what a client might assume is included. Delete the items that do not apply to this job.

Not included: [item], [item].

Anything not listed in this quote is not included in the price.

Then list what the price assumes. These are the conditions that must be true for your price to hold: access to the work area, working hours, materials the client supplies and the state of the existing work.

Assumptions

Use when the price depends on conditions you do not control. Keep only the lines that are true for this job.

The price assumes the following.

Access: we can reach the work area from [start time] to [finish time] on [days].
Materials: you supply [item] and have it on site by [date].
Existing work: the [wall, floor or pipework] is sound and needs no repair.
Services: power and water are on and free to use.

Changes to the job

Jobs change after the quote goes out. The client adds a socket or picks a dearer tile. You open a wall and find a problem. Write down in advance how this is handled: extra work is priced and agreed before it is done, and the total changes by the agreed amount.

Changes and extra work

Use on every quote. It covers changes the client asks for.

Changes: any extra work, or a change to the quantity or the specification above, is priced and agreed with you in writing before we do it. The total changes by the agreed amount.

Problems found during the work

Use on repairs, renovations and any job where part of the work is hidden. Change the examples to fit your trade.

Hidden problems: if we find a problem that could not be seen when we quoted, such as [rot, damp or old wiring], we will stop that part of the work and tell you. We will send a price for the extra work and carry on once you agree.

If the job changes before the client accepts, send a revised quotation that shows the new price and says what changed. After they accept, put the extra work in a short email and wait for a written yes before you start it.

Cancellation

Keep the cancellation clause short. Say what happens if the client cancels before the start date, and what happens once you have ordered materials or spent time on the job. Cancelling is the reverse of accepting, so keep the two clauses side by side. Wording for the acceptance side is in our quote acceptance wording.

One more thing matters when the client is a person buying work for their home. Citizens Advice tells customers in England that they have a 14-day cooling-off period to cancel building or decorating work they arranged by phone, online or away from the trader's premises, such as at their home. Inside those 14 days, the customer can cancel and get all their money back if the business has not started the work. The period starts the day after the customer gives the go-ahead. The page calls 14 days the absolute minimum a seller must give. It lists exceptions, such as specially made items, and urgent repairs or maintenance the customer asks for.

If the customer asks for the work to start inside that period, and the business has given the cancellation details, the customer pays a part of the agreed price for the work done. If the work starts without the customer asking for it, the customer can cancel and get a full refund. The business must give the customer details of how to cancel. If it does not, the cooling-off period is extended by 14 days from the date the customer receives them, up to a maximum of 1 year. Rules differ in other places, so check the ones where you work.

So give a home customer in England written details of how to cancel, with the quote. This covers a customer who agreed the work by phone, online or at their home. The page does not mention emailed quotes, so if the client accepts by replying to your email, treat that as agreeing online and give them the details too. Let your own cancellation charges apply only after the 14 days. Materials you order inside the 14 days are at your own risk. Even if the customer asked you to start sooner, they pay only for the part of the job completed when they cancel. The line 'This does not affect your legal rights' is a reminder. It does not replace those details.

Cooling-off period (home customers)

Use when the client is a home customer in England who agreed the work by phone, online or at their home. Send it with the quote and add your contact details. It follows the rule as Citizens Advice describes it for England, so check the rules where you work.

Cooling-off period: you have 14 days to cancel this work, starting the day after you give the go-ahead. If you cancel in that time and we have not started the work, you get all your money back.

If you ask us to start the work inside the 14 days and then cancel, you pay a part of the agreed price for the work done by then.

To cancel, contact us at [your contact details].

Cancelling before the work starts

Use on every job with a start date. The charges apply as written to business clients. For a home customer in England who agreed the work by phone, online or at their home, they apply only after the cooling-off period above. Fill in your hourly rate, or delete that sentence. The last sentence stays.

Cancellation: you can cancel this quote at any time before work starts by telling us in writing. If we have already ordered materials for you that we cannot return, you pay for them. If we have spent time on your job, you pay for that time at [hourly rate]. We refund the rest of your deposit. This does not affect your legal rights.

Sources checked 30 October 2026: Citizens Advice: Cancelling building or decorating work.

Payment: a deposit of £520.00 including VAT is due when you accept. It books the start date and pays for the materials. The balance of £993.20 is due within 7 days of our invoice, which we send when the job is finished. Pay by bank transfer.

Here is where each clause sits.

  • Valid until: the notes point to the calendar date at the top of the quote, so there is one date and no count of days.
  • Exclusions and assumptions: the notes list what is left out and the conditions behind the price. The tile allowance is stated per m², so a dearer tile changes the price in a way the client can see.
  • Payment: the deposit and the balance are amounts, and they add up to the total of £1,513.20. The deposit is enough to cover the materials in the quote, VAT included.
  • Changes: extra work is agreed in writing first, and a hidden problem behind the old tiles has its own sentence.
  • Cancellation: the client gets all their money back if they cancel inside the 14-day cooling-off period before work starts. After that, they pay only for materials you cannot return and for time already spent.

What to include in a handyman quote

A handyman quote covers many small jobs, so the client needs to see each one. Put each of these on the quote.

  • Your business name and contact details, the client's name, the job address, a quote number, the date and a valid-until date.
  • The job list, task by task, each with a short plain description.
  • A time estimate for each task, or the total time you expect to be on site.
  • Materials: what is needed, who buys it, and whether you bill it at cost with receipts or with a stated markup.
  • A minimum charge: the least you charge for a visit, such as one hour or a half day.
  • A trip or call-out charge, if you charge one.
  • What happens if a task is bigger than it looks: you stop, tell the client and agree the extra price in writing.
  • Disposal of old items and clean-up: included, or charged on a line of its own.
  • What is not included: gas, electrical and plumbing work that needs a registered or licensed trade, and any job not on the list.
  • A warranty on your work, and how long it lasts.
  • Payment: any deposit, the balance, when it is due and how to pay. Payment on completion suits small jobs.
  • Cancellation: for a home customer in England who agreed by phone, online or at home, the 14-day cooling-off period and how to cancel.
  • How to accept the quote.

Payment and deposit wording

Rules worth checking before you quote

Some jobs need a registered or licensed trade. Keep them off a handyman quote, or list them under Not included and tell the client which trade to call.

  • Gas: in Great Britain, anyone employed to work on gas appliances in a home must be a Gas Safe registered engineer, competent for that kind of gas work, says the Health and Safety Executive.
  • Cancelling: in England, Citizens Advice says a home customer who arranges the work by phone, online or at home has a 14-day cooling-off period, starting the day after they give the go-ahead. Give them details of how to cancel, or the period can run on for up to a year. Our quotation terms and conditions page has cooling-off wording to copy.
  • Electrical: in England, notifiable work includes a new consumer unit, a whole new circuit, and a new socket or light in the space around a bath or shower. Most repairs, replacements and maintenance jobs are not notifiable. The Planning Portal advises using an installer registered with a competent person scheme, who can self-certify the work. If the installer is not registered, notifiable work must be inspected and certified by building control or a registered third-party certifier. They must be told before the work starts.
  • US: ask your state's contractor licensing board what you may quote without a license. California's licensing board, for example, says that anyone who contracts for work valued at $1,000 or more for combined labor and materials costs, or for a project that needs a building permit, or who uses employee labor, must hold a license. Check the limit and the rules where you work.
  • US deposits: your state may also limit the deposit you can take on home improvement work. California's contractors board, for example, says the down payment should never exceed 10 percent of the contract price or $1,000, whichever is less. The same page lists one exception, for contractors with a blanket performance and payment bond on file with the board. Check your state's rule before you ask for a deposit.
  • US contracts: the same California page says there must be a written contract for home improvement projects over $500 in combined labor and materials costs, with specific information about the customer's rights. Check what yours must include before you rely on an accepted quote.

Rules can change. Check the current rules where you work before you quote.

Sources checked 1 November 2026: Health and Safety Executive: Domestic gas, frequently asked questions; Planning Portal: Electrics, building regulations general information; Contractors State License Board (California): What kind of contractor do I need; Contractors State License Board (California): Contracts and binding agreements; Citizens Advice: Cancelling building or decorating work.

Download the quote as a PDF and attach it to your own email, because QuotationMaker does not send emails. Keep the email short: the total, whether it includes tax, the valid-until date and how to accept. Our guide on sending a quote to a client has email wording to copy.

faq.q: What should a handyman quote include?
faq.a: Your details, the client's name and the job address, a quote number and dates, the jobs task by task, a time estimate, materials and who buys them, a minimum or call-out charge, what is not included, a warranty, payment terms and how to accept. The checklist on this page covers each one.

faq.q: How do I price a handyman job?
faq.a: Pick a method that fits the job: an hourly rate with a minimum charge, a flat price per task, a job list priced task by task, or a half-day or day rate. Bill materials at cost or with a stated markup, and show any trip charge on its own line. The table on this page shows how to display each method.

faq.q: Should a handyman charge a minimum or a call-out fee?
faq.a: It can help. A short visit costs the same travel time as a long one. Put the minimum charge or the call-out line on the quote, so the client sees it before the visit.

faq.q: Do I need a license to work as a handyman?
faq.a: Ask the licensing board in your state or country. California, for example, requires a license from a set job value, and for any job that needs a building permit or uses employees, as the rules section on this page explains. In Great Britain, gas work needs a Gas Safe registered engineer. Check the rules where you work before you quote.

faq.q: Is there a Word version of the handyman quote template?
faq.a: This page has a free online template with a PDF download and no Word file. Word, Excel and PDF files exist for the contractor and tradesman template, which is linked in the first section of this page.

faq.q: Do I charge VAT or sales tax on a handyman quote?
faq.a: In the UK, you charge VAT only if you are VAT registered. In the US, ask your state's tax agency which lines are taxable where you work. Type your own rate and tax name into the quote maker. If tax does not apply, set the rate to 0 and say so in the notes.

faq.q: How long should a handyman quote stay valid?
faq.a: Long enough for the client to decide, and short enough that your rates and prices are unlikely to change before they say yes. The examples here use 30 days for a UK list of odd jobs and 14 days for a US day-rate booking.

What to include in a carpentry quote

A carpentry or joinery quote should say what you will build or fit and what it is made from. It should also say who supplies each part and what state you leave the work in.

  • Who the quote is from and for, the address of the job, a quote number, the issue date and the date the price expires.
  • Each item or room, with measurements in metres or linear feet. Say whether the work is first fix or second fix in the UK, or rough or finish carpentry in the US.
  • The timber and boards, named by species or board type, such as softwood, hardwood, plywood or MDF, with the size and grade.
  • Who supplies the doors, hardware and ironmongery, and when anything the client supplies must be on site.
  • The finish the work is left in: bare, primed or ready for decorating, and whether painting is included.
  • Old work and waste: whether taking off, taking away and making good are in the price or priced separately.
  • Site protection and clean-up, the access you need and the hours you work.
  • Rot or damage found when old work comes out: whether you stop and quote the repair first, or price an allowance for it up front.
  • Extra work: how it is priced, how the client agrees to it in writing, and the rate for extra time.
  • The warranty: how long it lasts, what it covers and what it leaves out, such as natural movement of timber.
  • Money terms: the deposit if you take one, when the balance falls due, how to pay, and your payment details.
  • How the client accepts, and the date by which they must.
  • Cancellation, for a client having work done at home in England: the cooling-off period that may apply and how to cancel.

Rules worth checking before you quote

Building rules, permits and licensing can affect what a carpentry quote must cover. Find out which apply where you work. Then settle on the quote who handles any approval or permit application and who covers the cost.

  • Structure (England): GOV.UK describes Approved Document A as the building regulation in England covering the structural elements of a building. It says this edition covers the construction of the structural elements, including walls, floors and roofs. Ask building control before you quote structural work, such as new floor or roof timbers.
  • Approval: GOV.UK says people must check whether they need approval before they construct or change buildings in certain ways. Its list of alteration projects that might need approval includes replacing windows and doors. The list does not say which doors. Work that is not on it could need approval too, so check with a building control body if you cannot decide. GOV.UK tells homeowners they do not need to get approval themselves if they use someone registered with a competent person scheme. The page also points to separate rules for Scotland and Northern Ireland.
  • Cancellation (England): Citizens Advice says a home client has a cooling-off period of 14 days to cancel and get a refund. This applies when the work was arranged by phone, online, by mail order or away from the business, such as at home. The 14 days start the day after the client gives the go-ahead. A business has to give the client details of how to cancel. Without them, the time to cancel stretches by 14 days from the day the client receives the details, up to a maximum of 1 year.
  • United States, permits and licenses: ask your local building department which work needs a permit, and check your state's licensing rules. Take California's contractors board as an example. It says anyone who contracts for work valued at $1,000 or more for combined labor and materials costs must hold a license. It says the same for anyone who contracts for a project that needs a building permit, or who uses employee labor.
  • United States, deposits and contracts: check your state's rules on both before you set a deposit or write the contract. California's contractors board gives another example. It says a down payment on a home improvement job should never exceed 10 percent of the contract price or $1,000, whichever is less. It names one exception, for a contractor with a blanket performance and payment bond on file with the board. It also says there must be a written contract for all home improvement projects over $500 in combined labor and materials costs. That contract must include specific information about the homeowner's rights and responsibilities. The US example's deposit is below that limit, but the example does not include the information that contract must have.

faq.q: What should a carpentry quote include?
faq.a: Start with the job address, each item or room with its measurements, and whether the work is first fix or second fix. Name the timber and boards, and say who supplies the doors and hardware. Then state the finish, what happens to old work and waste, site protection, and what you do if you find rot or damage. End with changes, a warranty, payment terms, the date the price expires and how to accept. For a home client in England, add how they can cancel.

faq.q: How do I price a carpentry job?
faq.a: Match the method to the work. Doors can go by the piece, and trim or boards by the metre or linear foot. Hard-to-measure work can go by the day, and a built-in can be one fixed price. Decide whether you supply and fit or fit only. Put anything you cannot see yet, such as hidden rot, on an allowance line of its own. Write the method into each line, for example 'each' or 'per metre', so the client can follow the sums.

faq.q: What if I find rot or damage when old work comes out?
faq.a: You can pause that part of the job and quote the repair, then resume once the client accepts the quote in writing. Or you can put an allowance on the quote and bill the amount you actually find. The UK example takes the first route and the US example takes the second. Whichever you choose, say so in the notes before the work begins.

faq.q: Who should supply the doors and hardware?
faq.a: Either of you can, so say which on the quote. If the client supplies them, say they must be on site before you start and that you do not cover faulty or wrong-size items. If you supply them, list them on their own lines. In the UK example the client supplies the doors and you supply the hinges and latches.

faq.q: Is a carpentry estimate different from a quote?
faq.a: Some carpenters use the two words for the same document, and others keep 'estimate' for a price that can change. This template works for either. The quote maker always puts QUOTATION at the top of the PDF, so if your price can change, say so in the first line of the notes and name what could change it.

faq.q: Can I make a free carpentry quote online?
faq.a: Yes. The quote maker on this page works as a free carpenter quote template, with no signup. Fill in the lines, add your terms and download the PDF. The free PDF has a small 'Made with GetQuotationMaker.com' line at the bottom of each page.

faq.q: Is there a Word version of the carpentry quote template?
faq.a: No, not on this page. The quote maker here produces a PDF. Some other trade pages, such as the contractor and tradesman quote template, offer Word and Excel files that suit carpentry with a few edits.

faq.q: Do I charge VAT or sales tax on a carpentry quote?
faq.a: Only a VAT-registered business adds VAT to its prices, and our guide to VAT on quotes explains when that applies. In the US, your state's tax agency can tell you which parts of a carpentry job are taxable. Type the rate and tax name that fit your case into the quote maker. If no tax applies, enter 0 and add a line in the notes saying so.

What to include in a fence quote

A fence quote, also called a fencing quote, should say where the fence goes, how long and how high it is, and what it is made from. It should say what happens to the old fence and what the ground might hide. Then it shows the price in lines the client can follow.

  • Who the quote is from and for, the address of the job, a quote number, the issue date and the date the price expires.
  • The fence line: where each run starts and ends, and who has confirmed the boundary. Say whether you build on the line of the old fence or on a line the client marks.
  • The length and height of each run, measured on site, and the style: panels, closeboard, picket, chain-link, metal or vinyl.
  • Posts: the material and size, the spacing, how deep they go and whether they are set in concrete.
  • Gates: the width, the material, the hardware and whether you hang and adjust them.
  • The old fence: whether you take it down, where the waste goes and whether that is in the price.
  • Ground and access: slopes, steps, rock, roots and old concrete. State what the price assumes and which part is an allowance.
  • Buried pipes and cables: who checks for them before the posts go in.
  • Permits and neighbours: who applies for a permit if one is needed, and whether a neighbour has agreed to any work on a shared boundary.
  • The finish and the clean-up: stain, paint or preserver, and what you leave tidy.
  • Changes, warranty, payment terms, the valid-until date and how to accept.

If the price can move, open with a Price line that says the figure is an estimate and names what could change it. If it is fixed, say that the total is fixed for the work listed.

Rules worth checking before you quote

Planning rules, utility checks and consumer rights can change what a fence quote must say. The pages below come from a government planning service, a free national before-you-dig service and a consumer charity. Find out which rules apply where you work, then say in the quote who is responsible for each.

  • Height (England): the Planning Portal says you can put up, alter or take down a fence without applying for planning permission if it is next to a highway used by vehicles and no higher than one metre, or no higher than two metres elsewhere. The right does not apply to a listed building or its grounds, or to a boundary shared with a neighbouring listed building. An article 4 direction or a planning condition can also remove it, and in a conservation area you might need permission to take a fence down. The guidance is for England, and Wales may differ.
  • Buried pipes and cables (US): anyone who plans to dig should contact 811, or the state 811 center, a few business days before digging, according to the 811 site. It names installing fences among common projects and calls the service free. Put the request in your timetable and say who makes it.
  • Cancelling work arranged away from your premises (England): Citizens Advice describes a 14 day cooling-off period when work is arranged over the phone, on the internet, by mail order or anywhere outside the business, such as the customer's home. The period starts the day after the customer gives the go-ahead. The business must give details of how to cancel. If it does not, the period is extended by 14 days from the date the customer gets them, up to a maximum of 1 year. A customer who asks for the work to start inside the period, and then cancels, pays a part of the agreed price if the business gave those details. There may be no cooling-off period for something specially made. Put the cancellation details in the email that sends the quote, and decide whether to order materials before the 14 days end.

Sources checked 19 November 2026: Planning Portal: Fences, gates and garden walls, planning permission; 811: Before you dig, every dig, every time; Citizens Advice: Cancelling building or decorating work.

faq.q: What should a fence quote include?
faq.a: Start with the job address, the line of the fence and who has confirmed the boundary. Give the length and height of each run, the style, and the posts, gates and hardware. Say what happens to the old fence and what the ground may hide, with an allowance line for blocked post holes. End with what is not included, changes, payment terms, the date the price expires and how to accept.

faq.q: How do I price a fence job?
faq.a: Match the method to the work. A straight run can go at a price per metre or foot installed. A panel fence can go by the panel and the post. Gates and the removal of the old fence are usually fixed lines. Small repairs can go by the day. Put anything you cannot see yet, such as rock in the ground, on an allowance line of its own.

faq.q: Do I need planning permission for a fence?
faq.a: In England, the Planning Portal says you do not need to apply if the fence is no higher than one metre next to a highway used by vehicles, or no higher than two metres elsewhere. Listed buildings, article 4 directions and planning conditions can change that, and in a conservation area you might need permission to take a fence down. Check with your local planning authority before you quote. Rules in other countries differ.

faq.q: Can I use this as a fence estimate template?
faq.a: Yes. The layout is the same. If the price can move, open the notes with a Price line that says the figure is an estimate and names what could change it. If it is fixed, say that the total is fixed for the work listed.

faq.q: Do I add VAT or sales tax to a fence quote?
faq.a: That depends on where you work and on whether you are registered. For US sales tax, ask your state tax office, because the rules differ by state. Type your own rate and tax label in the quote maker, and set the rate to 0 if you charge no tax. The two examples use VAT for the UK and a sales tax for the US as illustrations only.

What to include in a tiling quote

A tiling quote should say which rooms or walls you will tile and how you measured them. It should say which tiles go on and who supplies them. Then it shows the work that comes before and after the tiles, because the client cannot see that work in a price per square metre.

  • Who the quote is from and for, the address of the job, a quote number, the issue date and the date the price expires.
  • The rooms, walls or floors to be tiled, and how you measured the area. Give the area in m² or square feet.
  • The tiles: size, type and finish, and who supplies them. If you supply them, say how much extra is in the quantity for cuts and breakage.
  • Adhesive and grout: the type, and the grout colour the client chose.
  • The surface: what you will remove, how you will level or repair it, and whether you add backer board or a screed.
  • Waterproofing: for showers, wet rooms and bathroom floors, the system and the area it covers, on a line of its own.
  • Movement joints, trims and edging, and silicone at the corners and where tile meets another surface.
  • The old tiles or floor covering: whether you take them out, where the waste goes and what happens if you find damage or something you cannot handle, such as suspected asbestos.
  • Access and working hours, the rooms that must be empty and the time the job takes.
  • Cleaning at the end, how long the client waits before using the floor or the shower, a warranty, payment terms, the valid-until date and how to accept.

The same layout serves as a tile installation estimate template or a tile estimate template. What changes is the first line of the notes. If the price can move, open with a Price line that says the figure is an estimate and names what could change it. If it is fixed, say that the total is fixed for the work listed.

Rules worth checking before you quote

Old buildings can hide health risks that change what a tiling quote must say, and consumer rights can change when you may order materials. The pages below come from two government agencies and a consumer charity. Find out which rules apply where you work, then put the matching line in the quote, as the examples above do.

  • Asbestos (UK): the Health and Safety Executive says asbestos can be found in any industrial or residential building built or refurbished before the year 2000. Its diagrams of where it can occur list vinyl floor tiles backed with asbestos paper and bitumen adhesive. If you lift old floor coverings in an older building, write in the quote that you stop if you suspect asbestos, and that testing and removal are not included.
  • Lead paint (US): under the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, anyone paid to perform work that disturbs painted surfaces in homes built before 1978 must be certified and use lead-safe work practices. The EPA page says this includes sole proprietorships. If your work will disturb paint in an older home, ask the age of the house before you quote.
  • Cancelling work arranged away from your premises (England): Citizens Advice describes a 14 day cooling-off period when work is arranged over the phone, on the internet, by mail order or anywhere outside the business, such as the customer's home. The period starts the day after the customer gives the go-ahead. The business must give details of how to cancel. If it does not, the period is extended by 14 days from the date the customer gets them, up to a maximum of 1 year. A customer who asks for the work to start inside the period, and then cancels, pays a part of the agreed price if the business gave those details. There may be no cooling-off period for something specially made. Put the cancellation details in the email that sends the quote, and decide whether to order tiles before the 14 days end.

faq.q: What should a tiling quote include?
faq.a: Start with the job address, the rooms or walls to be tiled and how you measured the area. Name the tiles, who supplies them and how much extra is allowed for cuts. Add lines for preparation, waterproofing, laying, grout and silicone. State what happens if you find damage, what is not included, the warranty, payment terms, the date the price expires and how to accept.

faq.q: How do I price a tiling job?
faq.a: Most tilers price by area, at a rate per square metre or square foot, for labour only or for supply and lay. Put preparation and waterproofing on lines of their own, because the area rate does not show that work. Small or awkward jobs can go by the day. Put anything you cannot see yet, such as a damaged screed, on an allowance line.

faq.q: How much extra tile should a quote allow for?
faq.a: There is no single figure. The amount depends on the tile size, the pattern and the shape of the room. Decide your own allowance for cuts and breakage, put it in the tile line, and write the percentage on the quote so the client knows what the extra covers. The examples on this page show one allowance as an illustration, and you replace it with your own.

faq.q: Can I use this as a tile installation estimate template?
faq.a: Yes. The layout is the same. If the price can move, open the notes with a Price line that says the figure is an estimate and names what could change it. If it is fixed, say that the total is fixed for the work listed.

faq.q: Do I add VAT or sales tax to a tiling quote?
faq.a: That depends on where you work and on whether you are registered. For US sales tax, ask your state tax office, because the rules differ by state. Type your own rate and tax label in the quote maker, and set the rate to 0 if you charge no tax. The two examples use VAT for the UK and a sales tax for the US as illustrations only.
